joins.before_text: We will build the arithmetic of these moves. It will tell us how to shorten a sequence, how to undo it, and which details we can forget without breaking the calculation. That last question will take us all the way to quotient groups.
joins.after_text: Our two machines produced different arrangements, but both tiles still fit their square frame. Let's collect every move with that property. We are tracking the colored corners, so turning a tile counts as a new move even though its outline looks unchanged.

joins.before_text: That gives four choices for blue, and then two choices for orange. Once those are fixed, the other two corners are forced: each has a particular adjacency to the first pair. There are at most eight arrangements. Our rack already contains eight different ones. That proves the list is complete.
joins.after_text: Now we can stop describing a move by the entire history of how we made it. Two sequences represent the same symmetry when they send every corner to the same destination. The machine might take a long route, but its final action is one of these eight.

joins.before_text: These requirements are not a ceremonial checklist. Closure makes calculations stay within our vocabulary. Associativity lets us package a long calculation into steps. The identity gives a neutral action. Inverses let us solve equations by undoing operations. Next we will see how these four properties make deductions possible without knowing what the objects are made of.
joins.after_text: It is eleven o'clock. Five hours pass. Where will the marker land?

joins.before_text: Those numbers have not become equal as integers. They are equivalent for this particular purpose: each differs from four by a whole number of twelve-hour trips. If we were counting hours actually worked, four and sixteen would not be interchangeable. What counts as the same depends on the question.
joins.after_text: The square gave us the group requirements. Now test them in a different machine: clock arithmetic. Start with a collection of moves and a rule for combining two of them. For the twelve-hour clock, the moves are advances by zero through eleven hours, and combining them means adding modulo twelve.

joins.before_text: To undo a sequence, reverse its order and undo each move. If the product is a b, its inverse is b inverse a inverse. In the combined expression, b meets b inverse in the middle, then a meets a inverse. The cancellations work because we reversed the order, not because we were allowed to commute the moves. These deductions apply to every group. Now we can ask when a smaller collection of moves forms a group of its own.
joins.after_text: What happens if we keep only the four rotations of the square? Combining two rotations gives another rotation, the do-nothing move stays, and every rotation can be undone by another one. This smaller collection is a group using the same operation. It is a subgroup of the square's symmetry group.

joins.before_text: That gives closure, the identity and inverses. Associativity comes for free, because we are still using the operation of the big group. And every subgroup passes the test, so the test is exactly right. Now let's meet our four-move subgroup again, through a question about order.
joins.after_text: Pick the horizontal flip s. Which of the eight square symmetries can we exchange with that flip without changing the result? Compare the two orders, and follow the numbered corners. What do you predict?

joins.before_text: Now ask for more. Which moves commute with every move? That set is called the center. A move in the center must put all four mirror lines back where they were. Only the identity and the half-turn do that, and both commute with every rotation as well. The center is what all the centralizers have in common.
joins.after_text: A cyclic group begins with a single move. Repeat it, run it backwards, and include doing nothing. Every position you can reach in this way belongs to the subgroup generated by that move. On our twelve-hour clock, let's use the move add eight. Before we calculate, predict how many different positions this move can visit.

joins.before_text: The visual lesson is that repeating a move produces an orbit, and the first return measures its order. The arithmetic of greatest common divisors predicts that return on a clock. The subgroup proof works much more generally: divide exponents, then use the smallest positive step to rule out a remainder. Next we will make the moves themselves into permutations of labelled objects.
joins.after_text: A permutation is a rearrangement that sends each item to exactly one position, with no collisions and no missing destinations. Imagine four numbered cards. We can describe a rearrangement by tracking where each label goes. Let's follow card one to its new position, then the card it displaced, until the trail closes.

joins.before_text: A composition predicts the combined effect, and the inverse tells us how to undo it. Here, seven more out-shuffles undo the first. The group records what the moves do; it does not by itself guarantee that a physical device performs them without error. Suppose two neighboring cards trade places during one shuffle. That is one extra swap, so the eight shuffles now end on an odd permutation, and doing nothing is even, so the deck cannot be home. Next we'll ask when two groups with different-looking objects actually have the same structure.
joins.after_text: The clock positions zero, one, two and three do not look much like rotations of a square. Yet the two systems can have exactly the same pattern of combinations. Think of a dictionary that translates every clock move into one square rotation and translates the results back without changing how combination works.

joins.before_text: An automorphism is an isomorphism from a group back to itself: a relabelling that preserves every combination. For a four-clock, sending a position to its negative is an example; it exchanges one and three while fixing zero and two. These translations let us recognize shared structure across different representations. Next we will use equivalence classes to organize an entire group into equally sized pieces.
joins.after_text: Imagine sorting integers by where they land on the twelve-hour clock. We will put numbers landing at four into one lane, and numbers landing at five into another.

joins.before_text: And if the first integer matches the second, and the second matches the third, add their two differences. The first and third differ by a multiple of twelve as well. These three properties are called reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
joins.after_text: Now change the rule. Call two integers close when they are at most one apart. Zero is close to one, and one is close to two.

joins.before_text: Groups will do the same thing. A subgroup will define an equivalence relation. Its classes will be called cosets. And for the right kind of subgroup, those classes will become the elements of a new group.
joins.after_text: On a twelve-position clock, start at zero and repeatedly add four. You visit zero, four, and eight before returning. These three positions form a subgroup H. Now move the whole pattern forward by one: the new set is one, five, and nine. Move it forward by two, or by three, to make two more patterns. These shifted copies are called cosets.

joins.before_text: Before we return to that question, we can combine two groups in a different way. Put two clocks side by side, and let a move turn each clock independently. The resulting pairs form a direct product. We can calculate in each coordinate and watch how two separate cycles combine into one longer orbit.
joins.after_text: Imagine two clocks side by side. The first has four positions, the second has three. A state is an ordered pair: one position on the first clock and one on the second. There are four choices for the first coordinate and three for the second, so the combined system has twelve states. The order of the coordinates matters because they belong to different clocks.

joins.before_text: Next we return to the cosets we made earlier. They partition a group, but can we use them as the elements of a new group? We will try multiplying two cosets in the square symmetries and discover exactly why some subgroups allow the operation and others do not.
joins.after_text: The cosets of a subgroup divide the group into equally sized pieces. It is tempting to treat each piece as one new object and multiply pieces by multiplying representatives. But a piece has many representatives. Before this can define an operation, every choice must lead to the same result. Let's see a failure using the square symmetries we already know.

joins.before_text: As a final test, ask what the projection sends every rotation to. They all land in the identity coset R. What does it send any reflection to? The other coset. The rotations are exactly the elements mapped to the identity; this set is called the kernel of the projection. Kernels are normal, which is why quotients and operation-preserving maps naturally fit together.
joins.after_text: Abstract structure becomes useful when it captures the feature we need to test. As one example, consider the older ten-digit ISBN system. Modern ISBNs have thirteen digits and use a different check, but the older system gives us a particularly clean example. This is not a security system: it is an arithmetic check that catches particular copying errors. Its arithmetic happens modulo eleven, and its weighted sum is built from the additive group of residues modulo eleven.
